DECL_PORT.trigger: An occurrence is DECL_PORT when the element is declared by a port declaration in the port clause of the entity being read.
DECL_PORT.context: Inside the port clause of the entity declaration; that port clause is in its Context (section D). The `<dir>` indicates the direction of the interface; it can be in, out, inout, buffer or linkage. Several identifiers can share one entry, and each of them is then an element of its own. A generic clause, `generic ( ... );`, comes before the port clause. A `port map (` in an instantiation is not a port clause.
exclusion: An entry in the port clause of a component declaration declares a port of a different entity. It is not an occurrence of the element: write no entry.
An entry in a generic clause has no <dir> and declares a constant, not a port. A generic is not an element: write no entry.
basis: The statement declares one element of the entity's external interface.
The `<dir>` indicates the direction of the interface; it can be in, out, inout or buffer.
Several identifiers can share one entry, and each of them is then an element of its own:
Context: The statements appear inside a port clause, which holds the interface list.
A port clause appears in an entity declaration.
It also appears in a component declaration, which describes the interface of a different entity, so those entries are not elements of the entity being read.
A generic clause has a similar shape but declares constants and carries no `<dir>`, which is what tells the two apart.

DECL_SIGNAL.trigger: An occurrence is DECL_SIGNAL when it names a signal being declared with a signal declaration statement.
DECL_SIGNAL.context: The signal has no direction. Appears in a declarative part: the region of a construct where things are declared, before the construct's statements. A signal declaration can sit in the declarative part of an architecture, of an entity, of a block statement or of a generate statement, or in a package declaration. The declarative part of a process block and that of a function or procedure cannot hold a signal declaration; they declare variables. Section D gives the lines of the architecture declarative part.
exclusion: A declaration inside a process block or a subprogram declares a variable, not a signal. It is not an occurrence of a signal element: write no entry.
basis: The statement declares an internal signal that can be used to carry values between parts of a design.
The signal has no direction.
A signal can be given a starting value, written after the type:
Context: The statement appears in a declarative part, which is the region of a construct where things are declared, before any of its statements.
Normally that is the architecture's declarative part, between the architecture header and the `begin` of its body:
A process block and a subprogram cannot: those declare `variable`s, which are not signals.

PROCESS_TRIG.trigger: An occurrence is PROCESS_TRIG when the element is named in the sensitivity list of a process statement header.
PROCESS_TRIG.context: Always in the process statement header, the first line of a process block. The `element_label`s inside the `( )` are called the sensitivity list. It is a list of signals whose events trigger process execution. The process block is a block of sequential statements.
exclusion: The <process_label> is a label, not an element, and gets no entry. An element in the sensitivity list of a process written without a label is still PROCESS_TRIG.
In `process (all)`, the word all names no element, so that header gives no element PROCESS_TRIG.
An element used inside the process block, below the header, is not PROCESS_TRIG there.
basis: The element appears in the sensitivity list of a process statement header.
the `element_label`s inside the `( )` are called the sensitivity list. It is a list of signals whose events trigger process execution.
A process statement can be written without a `<process_label>`, and a sensitivity list can be written as `process (all)`.
Neither form names an element, so neither gives an element this site.
Context: Always appears in the process statement header, at the start of a process block.
The process block is a block of sequential statements: it starts with the process statement header and ends with:
The `<process_label>` is repeated at the end only where the header carries one.

EDGE_CHECK.trigger: An occurrence is EDGE_CHECK when the element is the argument of rising_edge(...) or falling_edge(...) in the condition of an if or an elsif.
EDGE_CHECK.context: The `element_label` inside the edge function is the edge condition of that branch. Always inside a process block; the Context includes the if statement and the branch the edge condition opens (section D). That branch is entered only at that edge.
exclusion: An element in the condition of an if or an elsif that is not inside rising_edge(...) or falling_edge(...) is IF_COND instead.
The same element named in the sensitivity list of the process header is a separate occurrence, on the header line, with its own PROCESS_TRIG entry.
basis: The element is the argument of an edge function in the condition of an `if` or an `elsif`.
The edge function, `rising_edge(...)` or `falling_edge(...)`, is what identifies this site.
The `element_label` inside it is the **edge condition** of that branch.
Whether the element is also named in the sensitivity list is recorded by its own site and is no part of this one.
Context: Always appears inside a process block. The branch the edge condition opens is entered only at that edge. A process that holds an edge condition is a clocked process.

DECL_FIELD.trigger: An occurrence is DECL_FIELD when the element is a field of a record-typed port or signal, and the occurrence is the statement that declares its base: the port declaration or the signal declaration of the base. It is the field's first entry, and the field gets DECL_FIELD nowhere else.
DECL_FIELD.context: A record groups several named fields under one name, so the field has no declaration statement of its own. A field is written with the base and the field name joined by a dot: `<base_label>.<field_label>`. DECL_FIELD is on the line of the statement that declares the base, inside the port clause or the declarative part that holds it; that port clause or declarative part is in its Context (section D). The record type is declared either in this source, in a `type <record_type> is record ... end record;` block, or outside it, in a package; say which in the Role. The record type declaration only gives the field its type; DECL_FIELD is not recorded there.
exclusion: At <base_label>.<field_label> in any other statement, the field does not get DECL_FIELD. The field gets its SITEs as any other element does in that statement: its primary SITE where one matches, with PART_SELECT where only a range of the field is used; a field slice that is the whole right-hand side of a signal assignment gets PART_SELECT alone. The base gets FIELD_USE.
A field line inside `type <record_type> is record ... end record;` is not an occurrence of the element: write no entry.
basis: The element is one field of a record-typed port or signal.
A record groups several named fields under one name, so the field has no declaration statement of its own.
Its declaration is the statement that declares the base, and its type comes from the record type:
This site is recorded on the field.
Context: The record type is declared either in this source, or outside it, in a package.
Record which of the two it is.
The base itself is declared by a port declaration statement or a signal declaration statement.
What the occurrence does there belongs to the field; this site records on the base that one of its fields was reached, and which one.
A field is written with the base and the field name joined by a dot: `<element_label>.<field_label>`.

IF_COND.trigger: An occurrence is IF_COND when the element is in the condition of an if or an elsif, and not inside rising_edge(...) or falling_edge(...).
IF_COND.context: The condition can test the `<element_label>` against a fixed value, against another element, or on its own. Always inside a process block (or a function or procedure), because an if statement is a sequential statement; the Context includes the if statement and the branch the condition opens (section D). The same process block can also hold an EDGE_CHECK, before or after this condition.
exclusion: An element inside rising_edge(...) or falling_edge(...) in the condition is EDGE_CHECK instead.

The condition of an `if ... generate` is not IF_COND. An if ... generate is a concurrent statement: it is written outside every process block and ends with end generate, not end if. No SITE covers its condition, so an element in it is an occurrence with an empty SITE Tagged list.
basis: The element is in the condition of an `if` or an `elsif` statement, and not inside an edge function.
The condition can test the `<element_label>` against a fixed value, against another element, or on its own.
What identifies this site is that the condition holds no edge function: a condition with `rising_edge(...)` or `falling_edge(...)` is EDGE_CHECK.

Context: Always appears inside a process block (or a function or procedure), because an `if` statement is a sequential statement. The same process block can also hold an EDGE_CHECK, before or after this condition. An `if ... generate` is a different statement and is not this site.

WHEN_COND.trigger: An occurrence is WHEN_COND when the element is in the condition written after when in a conditional signal assignment.
WHEN_COND.context: The condition is written to the right of `<=`, beside the values, inside the `when`'s condition, but it is not a value the `<target_label>` can take. It decides which of the values the `<target_label>` takes. Normally a concurrent statement in the architecture body, outside every process block.
exclusion: An element in the chosen expression or the alternative expression of a conditional signal assignment is WHEN_EXPR, not WHEN_COND.
The when of a case alternative, `when <choice> =>`, is followed by => and has no else: an element there is CASE_COND, not WHEN_COND.
basis: The element is the condition of a conditional signal assignment statement.

The condition is written to the right of `<=`, beside the values, inside the `when`'s condition , but it is not a value the `<target_label>` can take. It decides which of the values the `<target_label>` takes.
Context: Normally a concurrent statement in the architecture body, outside every process block.
It decides which of the values the `<target_label>` takes.

LHS_PROC.trigger: An occurrence is LHS_PROC when the element is the target, on the left of <=, of a signal assignment written inside a process block.
LHS_PROC.context: The statement is a sequential statement, so it is always inside a process block. The Context lists every branch and case alternative that encloses the statement, with what opened it (section D). This site does not say which kind of branch it is; that is read from the Context at a later stage.
exclusion: The target of a signal assignment written outside every process block is LHS_CONC instead.

An element that gives a position inside the parentheses of the target, as in <array_label>(<element_label>) <= <expression>;, is not the target: only <array_label> is. That element gets no LHS_PROC or LHS_CONC, and no other primary SITE from the target. Its add-on SITEs are written alone: INDEX, with PART_SELECT where a range of it is used; ATTR_PREFIX where it is written <element_label>'<attribute>; FIELD_USE for a record base written there as <element_label>.<field_label>.
basis: The element is the target of a signal assignment statement written inside a process block.
The `<element_label>` is on the left of `<=`.
The statement is a sequential statement, so it is written inside a process block, where it can sit inside the branch of an `if` statement:
Context: Always appears inside a process block.
Record the lines of every branch that encloses the statement: a branch opened by an EDGE_CHECK, a branch opened by an IF_COND, or none.
This site does not say which kind of branch it is; that is read from those lines at a later stage.

LHS_CONC.trigger: An occurrence is LHS_CONC when it is the target (left-hand side) of a signal assignment written outside any process block (a concurrent assignment in the architecture body).
LHS_CONC.context: Appears in the architecture body, outside every process block; it can sit inside a generate statement. No `if` statement encloses it, because an `if` statement is only written inside a process block (or a function or procedure); an `if ... generate` is a generate statement.
exclusion: The target of a sequential signal assignment inside a process block is LHS_PROC instead.

An element that gives a position inside the parentheses of the target, as in <array_label>(<element_label>) <= <expression>;, is not the target: only <array_label> is. That element gets no LHS_PROC or LHS_CONC, and no other primary SITE from the target. Its add-on SITEs are written alone: INDEX, with PART_SELECT where a range of it is used; ATTR_PREFIX where it is written <element_label>'<attribute>; FIELD_USE for a record base written there as <element_label>.<field_label>.
basis: The element is the target of a signal assignment statement written outside every process block.
The `<element_label>` is on the left of `<=`. The statement is a concurrent statement, written directly in the architecture body:
A conditional signal assignment written there is this site too, with the `<element_label>` as its target:

Context: Always appears in the architecture body, outside every process block. No `if` statement encloses it, because an `if` statement is only written inside a process block; an `if ... generate` is a different statement.

DIRR_ASS.trigger: An occurrence is DIRR_ASS when the element is the whole right-hand side of a signal assignment: no operator, no index, no range and no other name appears to the right of <=.
DIRR_ASS.context: Appears as a concurrent statement in the architecture body, or as a sequential statement inside a process block. Both sides have the same type and the same width.
exclusion: In a conditional signal assignment, an element in the chosen or the alternative expression is WHEN_EXPR instead, and an element in the condition is WHEN_COND.
Where the right-hand side joins the element to something else by an operator, it is RHS_OPERAND instead.

Where the element on the right-hand side carries an index or a range, it is not the whole right-hand side, so it is not DIRR_ASS: an index makes it INDEXED_NAME, a range makes it PART_SELECT, each written alone where no primary SITE matches.
Where the right-hand-side occurrence is an argument of a function call or a type conversion and is outside array positions and slice ranges, it is RHS_OPERAND instead.
basis: The element is the whole right hand side of a signal assignment statement.
No operator, no index, no range and no other name appears to the right of `<=`.
Context: Appears as a concurrent statement in the architecture body, or as a sequential statement inside a process block. Both sides have the same type and the same width.
Context: Recorded together with the site of the occurrence it appears in, not instead of it. It says which bits are used, not what the occurrence does.

WHEN_EXPR.trigger: An occurrence is WHEN_EXPR when it appears anywhere inside the chosen expression or the alternative expression of a conditional signal assignment (but not inside the condition), whether used alone or with operators.
WHEN_EXPR.context: The chosen expression is the value the `<target_label>` takes when the `<condition>` holds. The alternative expression is the value it takes otherwise. The condition and both expressions sit to the right of `<=` in one conditional signal assignment statement (normally a concurrent statement in the architecture body). A chain of conditions, `... when <condition1> else ... when <condition2> else ...`, has one chosen expression for each condition and one alternative expression at the end.
exclusion: An element in the `when` condition is WHEN_COND instead.
In a signal assignment that is not conditional, DIRR_ASS or RHS_OPERAND applies instead.
An element that gives an array position inside the chosen or the alternative expression is still WHEN_EXPR, and also INDEX: write both in the same entry.
basis: The element appears in the chosen expression or the alternative expression of a conditional signal assignment statement.
An element anywhere inside either one is this site:
This holds whether the `<element_label>` is used whole or joined to something else by operators. An element in the `<condition>` is WHEN_COND, not this site.

Context: The `<condition>` and both expressions sit to the right of `<=` in one statement. A chain of conditions, `... when <condition1> else ... when <condition2> else ...`, has one chosen expression for each condition and one alternative expression at the end.
The chosen expression is the value the `<target_label>` takes when the `<condition>` holds. The alternative expression is the value it takes otherwise.

CASE_EXPR.trigger: An occurrence is CASE_EXPR when the element is in the case expression of a case statement: the expression written between case and is, whose value picks the alternative that runs.
required_structure:
case <element_label> is
  when <choice> =>
    <sequential_statements>
  when others =>
    <sequential_statements>
end case;
CASE_EXPR.context: A case statement is a sequential statement, so it is always inside a process block (or a function or procedure); written outside every process block it is not valid VHDL. The case expression is on the case line; the Context includes the case statement (section D).
exclusion: An element inside a choice, between when and =>, is CASE_COND instead.
An element in the statements of an alternative is not CASE_EXPR: it gets the SITE of its own statement, for example LHS_PROC, DIRR_ASS, RHS_OPERAND or IF_COND.
A literal or a named constant written as the case expression is not an element: write no entry for it.

The expression after with in a selected signal assignment, `with <expression> select <target_label> <= <expression> when <choice>, <expression> when others;`, is a different statement and is not CASE_EXPR. No SITE covers it, so an element there is an occurrence with an empty SITE Tagged list.

Where only a range of the element's bits is the case expression, PART_SELECT is written together with CASE_EXPR. Where the case expression is <base_label>.<field_label>, the field gets CASE_EXPR and the base gets FIELD_USE.

CASE_COND.trigger: An occurrence is CASE_COND when the element is written inside a choice of a case statement, between when and =>. A choice must be locally static, so an element can appear there only as the prefix of an attribute with a fixed value, such as <element_label>'length or <element_label>'high.
CASE_COND.context: Always inside a case statement, so always inside a process block (or a function or procedure). The Context includes the case statement and the alternative the choice starts (section D).
exclusion: An element written alone as a choice, `when <element_label> =>`, is not valid VHDL: a choice must be locally static, and the compiler rejects a signal there.
A choice that is a literal, a named constant, an enumeration value, others, or a range or a `|` list of them holds no element: write no entry for it.
The element in the case expression, between case and is, is CASE_EXPR instead.

The when of a conditional signal assignment, `<target_label> <= <chosen_expression> when <condition> else <alternative_expression>;`, has a condition and an else, not a choice and =>: an element there is WHEN_COND, not CASE_COND.

A choice of a selected signal assignment, `with <expression> select <target_label> <= <expression> when <choice>, <expression> when others;`, is a different statement and is not CASE_COND. No SITE covers it, so an element there is an occurrence with an empty SITE Tagged list.
An element in the statements of the alternative a choice starts gets the SITE of its own statement, not CASE_COND.
The element in <element_label>'<attribute> inside a choice gets CASE_COND together with ATTR_PREFIX.

RHS_OPERAND.trigger: An occurrence is RHS_OPERAND when the element is joined to something else by an operator on the right-hand side of a signal assignment that is not conditional, or is an argument of a function call or a type conversion on that right-hand side, outside array positions and slice ranges, with or without an operator.
RHS_OPERAND.context: An `<operator>` is a symbol or word such as `and`, `or`, `not`, `xor`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `/=` or `&`. Appears as a concurrent statement in the architecture body, or as a sequential statement inside a process block.
exclusion: In a conditional signal assignment, an element in the chosen or the alternative expression is WHEN_EXPR instead, and an element in the condition is WHEN_COND.
Where the right-hand side is exactly the element and nothing else, it is DIRR_ASS instead.

An element joined to something else by an operator within its innermost enclosing array position or slice range on the right-hand side matches RHS_OPERAND. Write the matching add-on SITEs in the same entry: INDEX for a position value or ATTR_PREFIX for an attribute prefix, with PART_SELECT where a range of the element is used.

The name before the parentheses must be a function or a type, not an element: with an element array before the parentheses, <array_label>(<element_label>), the array is INDEXED_NAME and the element inside is INDEX.
basis: The element is joined to something else by operators on the right hand side of a signal assignment statement.
An `<operator>` is a symbol or word such as `and`, `or`, `not`, `xor`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `/=` or `&`.
An expression built from operators is combinational logic: its result depends only on the current values of its inputs.
Context: Appears as a concurrent statement in the architecture body, or as a sequential statement inside a process block. In a conditional signal assignment, the element is WHEN_EXPR instead.

VAR_RHS_OPERAND.trigger: An occurrence is VAR_RHS_OPERAND when the element is joined to something else by an operator on the right-hand side of a variable assignment, which is written with :=, or is an argument of a function call or a type conversion on that right-hand side, outside array positions and slice ranges, with or without an operator.
VAR_RHS_OPERAND.context: A variable assignment is a sequential statement, inside a process block, a function or a procedure.
exclusion: A signal assignment, written with <=, is RHS_OPERAND instead.
An element that is the whole right-hand side of a variable assignment, with no operator, is not VAR_RHS_OPERAND. No SITE covers it, so it is an occurrence with an empty SITE Tagged list.
The variable itself is not an element: write no entry for it.
A := in a declaration gives a starting value; it is not a variable assignment.

ASSOC_ACTUAL.trigger: An occurrence is ASSOC_ACTUAL when the element is in the actual part of an association element in the port map or the generic map of an instantiation: to the right of => in a named association, or an entry of a positional association list.
ASSOC_ACTUAL.context: Inside the association list of an instantiation, `<instance_label> : <unit_name> ... port map ( ... );`; the Context includes that association list (section D). Name, in the Role, the formal the element is associated with.
exclusion: The formal part, to the left of =>, names a port or a generic of the instantiated unit, not the element: write no entry for it.
The word open as an actual is not an element: write no entry.

An element inside the argument of a function call or a type conversion in a statement, as in to_integer(unsigned(<element_label>)), is not ASSOC_ACTUAL: it keeps the SITE of the place where the call sits.
A port map is not a signal assignment: an actual is not DIRR_ASS or RHS_OPERAND.
Where the actual is <base_label>.<field_label>, the field gets ASSOC_ACTUAL and the base gets FIELD_USE. An index on the actual adds INDEXED_NAME to the same entry, a range adds PART_SELECT.

INDEXED_NAME.trigger: An occurrence is INDEXED_NAME when the element is the prefix of an indexed name: the array written before parentheses that hold one position.
INDEXED_NAME.context: Written wherever the indexed name sits: as a target, on a right-hand side, in a condition, in a case expression, or as an actual. An add-on SITE: written in the same entry as the primary SITE of the occurrence, or alone where no primary SITE matches (see the conflict rule for primary and add-on SITEs).
exclusion: An element inside the parentheses is INDEX, or ATTR_PREFIX where it is written as <element_label>'<attribute>.
A range in the parentheses, (<high> downto <low>) or (<low> to <high>), makes a slice name, not an indexed name: the prefix is PART_SELECT.
A named constant array, a function name or a type name before parentheses is not an element: write no entry for it.

INDEX.trigger: An occurrence is INDEX when the element is inside the parentheses of an indexed name: it gives the position of the item read from or written to an array.
INDEX.context: The `<element_label>` is not part of the value; it says which item of the array the value comes from or goes to. An add-on SITE: written in the same entry as the primary SITE of the occurrence, or alone where no primary SITE matches (see the conflict rule for primary and add-on SITEs). A `<conversion>` is a function such as `to_integer`, `unsigned` or `signed`. Conversions change how the same bits are read, not where they come from, and one conversion can wrap another. An array of arrays takes one position per level, `<array_label>(<index1>)(<index2>)`, and each element used as a position is this site.
exclusion: Where the position is a literal or a named constant, no element gives it: write no entry for it.
Where the <array_label> is a named constant, the constant is not an element: write no entry for it.
The array written before the parentheses is INDEXED_NAME, not INDEX.
An element written as <element_label>'<attribute> inside the parentheses is ATTR_PREFIX, not INDEX: the attribute's value gives the position, the element does not.
INDEX is an add-on SITE: write it in the same entry as the primary SITE of the occurrence, or alone where no primary SITE matches.

An element inside the parentheses of the target of a signal assignment, <array_label>(<element_label>) <= <expression>;, is not the target: it gets no LHS_PROC or LHS_CONC. Its add-on SITEs are written alone: INDEX, with PART_SELECT where a range of it is used.
basis: The element gives the position of the item read from or written to an array.
The `<element_label>` is not part of the value; it says which item of the array the value comes from or goes to.
The position can be written in several forms, and in each of them the `<element_label>` is this site:

A `<conversion>` is a function such as `to_integer`, `unsigned` or `signed`. Conversions change how the same bits are read, not where they come from, and one conversion can wrap another. An array of arrays takes one position per level, `<array_label>(<index1>)(<index2>)`, and each element used as a position is this site.

Context: Where the position is a literal or a named constant, no element gives it, so no element gets this site. Where the `<array_label>` is a named constant, the array is a table of fixed values, a read-only memory, and the constant is not an element.

ATTR_PREFIX.trigger: An occurrence is ATTR_PREFIX when the element is the prefix of an attribute name: written directly before an apostrophe and the attribute, as in <element_label>'left.
ATTR_PREFIX.context: The attribute gives a value about the element, such as its leftmost index for 'left; that value, not the element, is what the surrounding expression uses. An add-on SITE: written in the same entry as the primary SITE of the occurrence, or alone where no primary SITE matches (see the conflict rule for primary and add-on SITEs).
exclusion: It is not INDEX, even where the attribute's value gives an array position.
The same element written again as the array of the indexed name, as in <element_label>(<element_label>'left), is a separate occurrence with its own entry: that one is INDEXED_NAME.

PART_SELECT.trigger: An occurrence is PART_SELECT when the text uses a range of bits of an element (a part-select) rather than the whole element.
PART_SELECT.context: The syntax is a VHDL slice name, <element_label>(<high> downto <low>) or <element_label>(<low> to <high>); the taxonomy keeps the label PART_SELECT. It specifies which bits are used, not what the occurrence does. An add-on SITE: written in the same entry as the primary SITE of the occurrence, or alone where no primary SITE matches (see the conflict rule for primary and add-on SITEs). A slice that is the whole right-hand side of a signal assignment matches no primary SITE, so it is PART_SELECT alone.
exclusion: The prefix of an indexed name with one position, <element_label>(<expression>), is INDEXED_NAME, not PART_SELECT.
basis: Only a range of the element's bits is used.
Only those bits take part; the rest of the element does not.
Context: Recorded together with the site of the occurrence it appears in, not instead of it. It says which bits are used, not what the occurrence does.

FIELD_USE.trigger: An occurrence is FIELD_USE when the element is a record-typed base and the occurrence reaches one of its fields: the base in <element_label>.<field_label>.
FIELD_USE.context: The field is its own element entry; this site records on the base that one of its fields was reached, and which field. Name the field reached in the Role. FIELD_USE is always written alone on the base.
exclusion: At <element_label>.<field_label>, the base gets FIELD_USE and no other SITE from this occurrence. Write one FIELD_USE entry for each field reached.
The SITE for what the occurrence does goes in the field's own entry. That SITE is never DECL_FIELD: DECL_FIELD is recorded only on the line that declares the base.

Each field selection is its own occurrence: where the base appears several times on one line, as in (<base_label>.<field_label1> = <literal>) and (<base_label>.<field_label2> = <literal>), write one FIELD_USE entry for each.

An array whose elements are records, written <element_label>(<expression>).<field_label>, is not a record-typed base: the occurrence is an indexed name. The element gets INDEXED_NAME with the primary SITE of its position, for example LHS_PROC or LHS_CONC as the target, RHS_OPERAND or VAR_RHS_OPERAND on a right-hand side, or IF_COND in a condition, and no FIELD_USE.
basis: The element is a record-typed base, and this occurrence reaches one of its fields.
Name the `<field_label>` that was reached.

Context: The field is its own entry in the list of elements given to you. What the occurrence does there belongs to the field; this site records on the base that one of its fields was reached, and which one.
Its declaration is the statement that declares the base, and its type comes from the record type:

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: Every SITE is either primary or add-on, as its kind says. A primary SITE names the part of a statement or declaration the occurrence is in. Classify each written occurrence separately on its own side of the assignment delimiter <= or :=; do not transfer SITEs between repeated spellings. The target of a signal assignment is the name on the left of <= before the target's own parentheses. That prefix is outside those parentheses and gets LHS_PROC or LHS_CONC with INDEXED_NAME or PART_SELECT where written, never INDEX from its own parentheses. An element inside the target's parentheses is not the target and takes no primary SITE from it. An add-on SITE names how the name is written at that occurrence: a field reached, an array indexed, a position, an attribute, a slice. For each occurrence, first find its primary SITE; then test every add-on SITE separately, and write those that match in the same entry as the primary SITE. Where no primary SITE matches, write the add-on SITEs alone. FIELD_USE on a base is always written alone. In <element_label>(<expression>).<field_label> the element is an array indexed before a field is reached: it is INDEXED_NAME with its primary SITE, never FIELD_USE. Do not give an occurrence an add-on SITE because another name in the same statement has it.
When an element is in the condition of an if or an elsif: if the element is inside rising_edge(...) or falling_edge(...), the occurrence is EDGE_CHECK; otherwise it is IF_COND.
basis: The edge function, `rising_edge(...)` or `falling_edge(...)`, is what identifies this site.
The element is in the condition of an `if` or an `elsif` statement, and not inside an edge function.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: An element can have both a PROCESS_TRIG entry and an EDGE_CHECK entry, but never for the same statement, and never in the same entry. PROCESS_TRIG is written for the process statement header, where the element is named in the sensitivity list. EDGE_CHECK is written for the if or elsif statement inside that process block, where the element is the argument of rising_edge(...) or falling_edge(...). They are two separate occurrences, each with its own entry and its own line.
basis: Whether the element is also named in the sensitivity list is recorded by its own site and is no part of this one.
The element appears in the sensitivity list of a process statement header.
The element is the argument of an edge function in the condition of an `if` or an `elsif`.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: In a conditional signal assignment, an element inside the condition written after when is WHEN_COND; an element inside the chosen expression or the alternative expression is WHEN_EXPR.
basis: The element is the condition of a conditional signal assignment statement.
An element in the `<condition>` is WHEN_COND, not this site.
An element anywhere inside either one is this site:

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: If the assignment is a conditional signal assignment, elements in its expressions are WHEN_EXPR (not DIRR_ASS or RHS_OPERAND). For non-conditional assignments: if the right-hand side is exactly the element and nothing else (no operator, index, range, or other name) it is DIRR_ASS; if the right-hand side uses operators joining the element to others, the element is RHS_OPERAND; if the element is an argument of a function call or a type conversion on the right-hand side, outside array positions and slice ranges, it is RHS_OPERAND, with or without an operator.
basis: In a conditional signal assignment, the element is WHEN_EXPR instead.
No operator, no index, no range and no other name appears to the right of `<=`.
The element is joined to something else by operators on the right hand side of a signal assignment statement.
This holds whether the `<element_label>` is used whole or joined to something else by operators. An element in the `<condition>` is WHEN_COND, not this site.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: If the signal assignment target occurs inside a process block it is LHS_PROC; if it occurs outside every process block in the architecture body it is LHS_CONC.
basis: The element is the target of a signal assignment statement written inside a process block.
Context: Always appears inside a process block.
The element is the target of a signal assignment statement written outside every process block.
Context: Always appears in the architecture body, outside every process block.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: In <array_label>(<element_label>), the array is INDEXED_NAME and an element inside the parentheses is INDEX. Distinguish parentheses by the declared kind of the preceding name: an array introduces a position or slice range; a function or type introduces arguments. Call, conversion and grouping parentheses retain any enclosing array-position or slice-range scope. For RHS_OPERAND and VAR_RHS_OPERAND, an operator or call applied to an indexed name, slice or attribute value acts on the element prefix, not on occurrences inside position or range parentheses of that name. An operator or call inside those parentheses does not supply an operand SITE to the enclosing prefix. For an occurrence inside a position or range, require an operator that joins its value or attribute value to something else within its innermost enclosing position or range; a call or conversion alone does not qualify. A whole-right-hand-side indexed name or slice with no qualifying operator or enclosing call gets INDEXED_NAME or PART_SELECT alone. An element written as <element_label>'<attribute> inside the parentheses is ATTR_PREFIX, not INDEX. In <element_label>(<high> downto <low>), a slice, the prefix is PART_SELECT, not INDEXED_NAME. These four are add-on SITEs, each written in the entry of its own occurrence together with that occurrence's primary SITE: WHEN_EXPR inside a chosen or alternative expression, WHEN_COND inside a when condition, IF_COND inside an if or elsif condition, CASE_EXPR inside a case expression, RHS_OPERAND where an operator joins the occurrence to something else on the right-hand side of a signal assignment, LHS_PROC or LHS_CONC for the array or the slice that is itself the target, ASSOC_ACTUAL for an actual. An element inside the parentheses of a target is not the target, so it takes no LHS_PROC or LHS_CONC: its add-on SITEs (INDEX or ATTR_PREFIX, with PART_SELECT where a range of it is used) are written alone. Where no primary SITE matches, as for a bare position or a whole-right-hand-side slice, the add-on SITE is written alone. A literal or a named constant used as the position is not an element: write no entry for it.
basis: The element gives the position of the item read from or written to an array.
The `<element_label>` is not part of the value; it says which item of the array the value comes from or goes to.
An element anywhere inside either one is this site:
This holds whether the `<element_label>` is used whole or joined to something else by operators.
The element is in the condition of an `if` or an `elsif` statement, and not inside an edge function.
The element is the condition of a conditional signal assignment statement.
The element is joined to something else by operators on the right hand side of a signal assignment statement.
No operator, no index, no range and no other name appears to the right of `<=`.
Context: Where the position is a literal or a named constant, no element gives it, so no element gets this site.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: PART_SELECT is recorded together with the primary SITE of the occurrence where one matches (it is not an alternative site but an additional annotation naming which bits are used). A slice that is the whole right-hand side of a signal assignment matches no primary SITE, because DIRR_ASS needs no range and the slice is neither an operator operand nor a call or conversion argument: PART_SELECT is written alone there.
basis: Context: Recorded together with the site of the occurrence it appears in, not instead of it. It says which bits are used, not what the occurrence does.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: A field of a record-typed port or signal gets DECL_FIELD once, on the line of the statement that declares its base, and nowhere else. At <element_label>.<field_label> in any other statement, the base gets FIELD_USE, one entry for each field reached, and the field gets its SITEs as any other element does there: the primary SITE for what the occurrence does, where one matches (for example LHS_PROC, LHS_CONC, DIRR_ASS, RHS_OPERAND, WHEN_EXPR, WHEN_COND, IF_COND, CASE_EXPR, ASSOC_ACTUAL or VAR_RHS_OPERAND), and the add-on SITEs that match (INDEX, INDEXED_NAME, ATTR_PREFIX, PART_SELECT). A field slice that is the whole right-hand side of a signal assignment gets PART_SELECT alone. A field line inside a record type declaration is not an occurrence of the element: write no entry.
basis: Its declaration is the statement that declares the base, and its type comes from the record type:
This site is recorded on the field.
The base itself is declared by a port declaration statement or a signal declaration statement.
The element is a record-typed base, and this occurrence reaches one of its fields.
What the occurrence does there belongs to the field; this site records on the base that one of its fields was reached, and which one.
The field is its own entry in the list of elements given to you.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: An entry in the port clause of a component declaration describes the interface of a different entity. It is not an occurrence of the element being read: write no entry. Only an entry in the port clause of the entity being read is DECL_PORT.
basis: A port clause appears in an entity declaration.
It also appears in a component declaration, which describes the interface of a different entity, so those entries are not elements of the entity being read.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: In a case statement, an element between case and is is CASE_EXPR; an element inside a choice, between when and =>, is CASE_COND. The same element can have both entries, but never for the same part of the statement and never in the same entry: CASE_EXPR is written for the case line, CASE_COND for the when line of the alternative.

Both are written after a when. A when followed by a choice and => starts an alternative of a case statement: an element there is CASE_COND. A when followed by a condition and else is part of a conditional signal assignment: an element there is WHEN_COND.
basis: The element is the condition of a conditional signal assignment statement.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: Both decide which branch runs. An element in the case expression, between case and is, is CASE_EXPR. An element in the condition of an if or an elsif, between if or elsif and then, is IF_COND.
basis: The element is in the condition of an `if` or an `elsif` statement, and not inside an edge function.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: Being inside an alternative of a case statement is not a SITE. An element in a statement inside an alternative gets the SITE of that statement, not CASE_EXPR or CASE_COND. The alternative is part of the Context, as a structure of kind alternative (section D).
basis: Record the lines of every branch that encloses the statement: a branch opened by an EDGE_CHECK, a branch opened by an IF_COND, or none.

CONFLICT_RULES.rule: An element in the actual part of a port map or generic map association is ASSOC_ACTUAL. A port map is not a signal assignment, so the actual is not DIRR_ASS or RHS_OPERAND, and the formal to the left of => gets no entry.

Both cover an element joined to something else by an operator, or an argument of a function call or a type conversion outside array positions and slice ranges, on a right-hand side. Written with <=, a signal assignment, it is RHS_OPERAND; written with :=, a variable assignment, it is VAR_RHS_OPERAND.
